what: A first index of 120 PDFs went from 65.7 seconds to 3.0 - 22x - because the parser is now handed a batch instead of one file at a time. The documents that come out are asserted identical.

why_this_and_why_now.what_the_cache_left: The parse cache made a re-index nearly free and said so in its own record: 'the first build is unchanged - a cold corpus of a thousand PDFs is still minutes, because each one still starts a JVM.' This is that.
why_this_and_why_now.where_the_time_actually_was: Profiling the previous change put 99.2% of a PDF rebuild in opendataloader, and the shape of that cost is a Java process per document. Measured directly this time: ~640ms of the ~656ms a four-page PDF cost was the process starting up, leaving ~51ms of actual parsing.
why_this_and_why_now.who_pays_it: Every first index, every restore onto a new machine, and every install at the company this is built for - the one moment a new operator is watching.

measured.batch_size: 128 four-page PDFs, per document: one JVM per file 656ms, batches of 32 71ms, batches of 64 49ms, batches of 128 40ms. Almost the whole win is in not paying start-up per document; past a few dozen the curve is nearly flat. 64 takes ~13x of a possible ~16x and bounds both the files staged on disk and what the parser holds at once.
measured.a_measurement_that_was_noise: The first run made 32 look like the sweet spot and 64 slower. Re-run in the other order, 64 beat 32 consistently by ~20% - the first number was page-cache and JIT warm-up, not the batch size. Nothing was decided on the first reading.
measured.end_to_end: 120 one-page PDFs through the connector: one JVM per file 65.7s (548ms/doc), batched 3.1s (26ms/doc). 21x. A thousand policy PDFs: 9.1 minutes to about 25 seconds.
measured.with_the_cache: The two compose. Warm cache, batched: 0.02s for the same 120 documents, and no JVM starts at all - pinned by a test that counts convert() calls and asserts zero.
measured.correctness: Every document parses to exactly what it parsed to alone: blocks, title, pages and warnings, asserted per document. The whole corpus a scan produces is asserted identical with batching and without.
measured.bounded_rather_than_eager: The read-ahead is driven by the walk and runs one group ahead, not over the whole corpus first: a group holds every document in it in memory, and reading a thousand large PDFs before indexing any of them would trade a JVM problem for a memory one. The eager version measured 22x against this one's 21x - inside the noise, and not worth holding a second copy of a corpus for. A test counts what is actually held rather than trusting the comment.
measured.against_the_other_backend: Checked rather than assumed, because the Java parser is an optional extra: the Docker image installs it and a JVM, the Windows installer does not and never has. The same 120 PDFs through pdfplumber: 7.17s, 59.7 ms/doc. So a Windows install never had the JVM cost at all - the nine minutes was a Docker number. What changed is the ranking: OpenDataLoader was 11x slower than pdfplumber and chosen anyway for structure it reports rather than infers; batched it is 20.9 ms/doc, about 3x faster. The better parser is no longer the slow one.

two_things_that_would_have_been_silent.the_filename_collision: The CLI names each output after its input's basename. Batching HR/policy.pdf and Finance/policy.pdf by their real paths writes one policy.json - verified, two different PDFs with the same basename produced exactly one output file. That is a document silently lost, or worse, one policy answered out of another one's text. Every file is staged under a generated name instead, and the connector test that pins it goes through real paths, which is where the mistake would be reintroduced.
two_things_that_would_have_been_silent.the_bad_file: The CLI exits non-zero when any file in a batch is unreadable - but writes every good document first. So the failure is read rather than raised, and anything missing from the output is re-parsed on its own, where it produces the same sentence it would have produced had it never been batched. Without that, one corrupt PDF would have cost a whole batch.

a_defect_this_surfaced.what: The sentence an operator was shown for an unreadable PDF was 'OpenDataLoader could not read this PDF: Command [\'java\', \'-Djava.awt.headless=true\', ... ]' returned non-zero exit status 1' - a temp path, a jar path and an exit code, none of which anybody can act on.
a_defect_this_surfaced.found_by: A test asserting that a batched failure carries the same warning as an unbatched one. It did not: the two differed only in the random temp directory in the message, which is how it became visible that the message was a command line at all.
a_defect_this_surfaced.fixed: The wrapper's exception carries the CLI's own stdout, which says the useful thing. An operator now reads 'broken.pdf: OpenDataLoader: this file is not a valid PDF file (corrupted or truncated content).' The staged filename in the parser's sentence is replaced rather than shown - it is never the operator's filename.

structural_rather_than_tested: One private _convert is the only place that decides how the parser is invoked, so one document and sixty-four go through it identically. A batch that came to read a document differently from the single-file path would be invisible until a corpus grew past the batching threshold, and would then invalidate every cached answer on a re-index that changed nothing. A sabotage that made the batch pass different options is no longer expressible in one place - which is better than a test for it, and worth recording because the test written for it did not catch it: the synthetic PDFs carry no PDF/UA tags, so use_struct_tree changed nothing about their output.
every_test_was_checked_against_the_bug_i: Twelve sabotages, each applied and run: stage under the real basename, let a bad file abort the batch, never re-parse a missing output alone, the parser does not chunk, skip the pdfplumber rescue under auto, the read-ahead forgets to fill the cache, batch results land at the wrong index, read-ahead keys are not counted as seen, a group is read ahead even for pdfplumber, the read-ahead group is not bounded, the operator is told the java command line again, and the read-ahead hands back the wrong document. Three passed the first time and the tests were rewritten until every one failed. Two of those three were the same mistake twice, in mirror image: the connector splits groups and the parser splits batches, and a test that patched BOTH sizes proved only that *something* split. Each now patches one side and is pinned against that side alone.
gate: No retrieval, prompt, chunking or grounding change: the same parser, called in groups. The corpus a scan produces is asserted identical with batching and without, per document and whole. The golden sets gate answers, and no answer moved.
still_open: Batching only helps the Java backend; pdfplumber has no process to start and declines a batch. Uploads and deletes still rebuild the index, though the parse cache means they no longer re-parse. OCR for scanned PDFs is still unbuilt.
a_gap_this_made_worth_stating: TIMEOUT_SECONDS in documents/opendataloader.py has never been enforced: the wrapper package offers no timeout and runs the jar with a blocking subprocess.run, so the TimeoutExpired branch is unreachable and a PDF that never returns hangs an index. Batching makes a hang cost a whole group rather than one file. Fixing it means a timeout in the wrapper or spawning the jar here, which would duplicate the wrapper's job and drift with it - not attempted. The constant now says what is true rather than reading like a protection nobody has, and it is listed under known gaps.
